label: Real run on this Mac's Docker Compose stack, with synthetic traffic from klaxon.traffic: synthetic data, a simulated provider, no real money. One fault from klaxon.faults, provider-outage, was injected on purpose. The alert was raised by klaxon.alerts from what the stack showed. Klaxon's loop ran live on it, through Claude Code on Aravind's seat, and stopped on diagnosed after 10 steps; any reply it got is a recorded response, not a simulation. It was offered one write action (rollback_deploy), as in week 4; in an evaluation run its gate only plans an action the diagnosis names: nobody is asked, and nothing runs. The diagnosis was compared with the fault's recorded cause by a rule (klaxon.grading), not by a person or a model. Its diagnosis named no action, so nobody was asked to approve one. The fault's cause was removed by the harness's clearing: this fault's cause is not a deploy.

case.name: provider-outage
case.title: Payments fail: the provider hangs, and our circuit breaker fails fast
case.right_answer: The fault's recorded cause: the provider's charge and refund API hangs (5 s, then 503): our payments API's calls to it time out, each after 3 attempts, until its circuit breaker opens, after 5 calls in a row got no answer; from then on it fails fast, answering 503 'outcome unknown' at once without calling the provider, and lets one trial call through 10 s after it opened, and again after each trial that fails.
case.remedy: nothing to change on our side: the provider must recover (escalate to it). Meanwhile the circuit breaker keeps the API answering at once, and closes again when a trial call gets an answer. After it recovers, the payments and refunds left pending need a decision (retry them with their keys, or mark them failed): a refund left pending blocks new refunds on its payment until it settles

alert.name: PaymentsErrorsHigh
alert.summary: Payments are failing: over the last minute, 96% of the answers to POST /payments on payments-api were 5xx (8.90 per second), above the threshold of 20%. Payments are slow: over the last minute, the p95 latency of POST /payments on payments-api was 4.2 s, above the threshold of 2 s.

diagnosis.hypothesis: From ~16:47:58 the provider (fake-provider, outside party) stopped answering in time, though its container reports healthy. payments-api's /v1/payments and /v1/refunds calls hang until our ~3 s httpx read timeout (ReadTimeout, no_answer), and provider 200s fell to 0 by 16:48:43. Requests that reach the provider wait ~3 s (or ~6 s with two attempts) then fail, pushing p95 to ~4.2 s. The circuit breaker (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on) then opened, so most requests fail fast with 503 and the payment is left pending, giving ~96% 5xx. No change of ours lines up: all services were created at 16:46:16 with normal settings, so a rollback would not help. Open: why the provider is slow (it sends no logs); whether timed-out calls were processed on its side, leaving pending payments that may diverge; no money_check was run.

evidence.shows: payments-api ERRORs: 'provider unavailable; payment left pending'. The circuit breaker is open or half-open, after earlier attempts failed with ReadTimeout.
From 16:47:58, ReadTimeout/no_answer attempts rose to ~1.4–1.6/s on /v1/payments and ~0.2/s on /v1/refunds, while 200 answers fell from ~3/s to 0 by 16:48:43.

A POST /payments trace returned 503 after 3015 ms. Almost all of that was one POST to fake-provider:8000/v1/payments that failed after 3009 ms with httpx.ReadTimeout. Redis and Postgres spans were sub-millisecond.
Slow POST /payments and refund traces took ~3.0 s and ~6.2 s, matching one or two provider read timeouts per request.
The client latency histogram stays at ms levels, consistent with timed-out calls not being recorded there; it does not contradict the timeouts.
Every service was created once at 16:46:16 with expected settings (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents). No change of ours lines up with the 16:48 onset.
All containers running and healthy with 0 restarts, including fake-provider: its process is up but not answering in time.

proposed_fix.summary: No change on our side. 1) Escalate to the provider (or investigate fake-provider) and check its status. 2) Keep the circuit breaker on so POST /payments fails fast instead of hanging. 3) Once the provider recovers, run money_check(wait=true) to find timed-out calls the provider actually processed, and reconcile pending payments via webhooks or idempotent retries with their existing keys.

diagnosis.blast_radius: Taking no action leaves payments and refunds failing or pending until the provider recovers. Pending payments may diverge from the provider's records if timed-out calls were processed. Rolling back or restarting our services would add downtime without fixing anything.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: Nothing to undo, since no change is proposed. If a later mitigation changes timeout or breaker settings, revert to the settings recorded in the deploy log for 16:46:16.
